text: LORD, you are a God who avenges; O God who avenges, shine forth!

versions.text: The LORD is a God of vengeance; O God of vengeance, shine forth!
versions.explanation: Optional refinement: the Hebrew places YHWH as the addressee/subject in a vocative-like way, and 'God who avenges' reads more naturally aloud than the repeated noun phrase. Current rendering is acceptable, so this is only a stylistic suggestion.

text: Rise up, Judge of the earth; give the proud what they deserve.
How long, LORD, shall the wicked—how long shall the wicked exult?
They pour out arrogant words; all the evildoers boast.
They crush your people, LORD, and oppress your heritage.
They kill the widow and the stranger; they murder the fatherless.
And they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive."

versions.text: And they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob takes no notice."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb יבין means 'understand/perceive'; 'takes no notice' is a loose paraphrase. Also, verse 7 uses the short divine name יָהּ rather than the full name; a footnote noting 'Hebrew: Yah, a short form of the LORD's name' would help readers.

versions.text: And they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob pays no heed."
versions.explanation: The revision replaced 'takes no notice' with 'pays no heed,' but this repeats the very problem that prompted the change: יָבִין means 'understand / perceive,' not 'pay attention.' A cognitive verb ('does not perceive' or 'understands nothing') renders the Hebrew accurately and still reads smoothly aloud. A footnote on the divine name here (Hebrew 'Yah,' a short form of the LORD's name) would also still be helpful, as it has not yet been added.

text: Take heed, you senseless among the people; you fools, when will you understand?
He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?
He who disciplines the nations, will he not correct? Does he who teaches mankind knowledge not know?

versions.text: He who disciplines the nations, will he not rebuke? He who teaches humankind knowledge—
versions.explanation: The dangling dash at the end of v.10 forces the reader into v.11 mid-sentence, which hampers oral reading. Many read the second line as a complete rhetorical question. Consider closing the line so each verse stands as a readable unit.

text: The LORD knows the thoughts of man: they are only a breath.

versions.text: the LORD knows the thoughts of man: they are but a breath.
versions.explanation: If verse 10 is closed as a complete sentence, verse 11 should begin with a capital letter and stand independently. 'Only' also reads more naturally aloud than the archaic 'but a'.

text: Blessed is the one you discipline, LORD, the one you teach from your law,
giving him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.
For the LORD will not abandon his people; he will not forsake his heritage.
For justice will return to righteousness, and all the upright in heart will follow it.

versions.text: Judgment will again be just, and all the upright in heart will follow it.
versions.explanation: The opening כִּי ('for') links this verse to the preceding assurance and is omitted in the current rendering; restoring it preserves the logical flow.

text: Who will rise up for me against the wicked? Who will stand with me against the evildoers?
If the LORD had not been my help, I would soon have dwelt in the land of silence.
When I said, "My foot is slipping," your steadfast love, LORD, held me up.
When anxious thoughts filled my heart, your consolations brought joy to my soul.
Can a throne of destruction be allied with you—one that frames injustice into law?
They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn innocent blood.

versions.text: They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads 'innocent blood' (דָּם נָקִי) and the verb is 'condemn / declare guilty'; 'to death' is an addition not present in the text.

text: But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge.
He turns back on them their own iniquity and destroys them for their wickedness; the LORD our God destroys them.

versions.text: He will repay them for their wickedness and destroy them for their evil; the LORD our God will destroy them.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew 'turns back upon them their iniquity' expresses that their own evil recoils on them, which is lost in 'repay them for their wickedness.' Also אוֹנָם ('their iniquity') and רָעָתָם ('their evil') are rendered with the words reversed.
